offences.quote: Inappropriate use of artificial intelligence software or services in the completion of assessments. Assignment briefs will identify where use of artificial intelligence may be appropriate; in all other cases it is not.
Using another person's words or ideas without acknowledgement and submitting them for assessment as though it were your own work.
Fabrication of references, including references within the reference section or bibliography which have been fabricated and are not genuine sources.
Attempting to manipulate or evade academic integrity detection processes or software (e.g. Turnitin).
Use of services such as essay mills and/or any other agencies or commissioned academic work (either paid or unpaid).
Use of another person's words or ideas that has been slightly changed or paraphrased to make it look different from the original.

Possessing any unauthorised form of material such as a book, manuscript, data or loose papers, or bringing information obtained via an electronic device, or any other source of unauthorised information into an exam or assessment facility.
Work undertaken with others is submitted and passed off as solely the work of one person.
Impersonation of an examination candidate or allowing oneself to be impersonated.
Self-plagiarism – using your own work from a previous assignment/module when it has not been expressly permitted.

liability.quote: the offence must have occurred within the students first term and must only show minor examples of poor academic practice within the work.

just because you have a low Turnitin score, doesn't mean that your submission would not be scrutinised to check for correct academic practice.
notes or transcript from any interview regarding the allegations.

outcomes.quote: For all upheld cases of Academic Misconduct, students are now required to also complete a compulsory Academic Misconduct and Study Skills module.
There is an option for a School Level Warning, however there are specific criteria to allow this to be issued

Normally for a first offence, it is likely a student would be offered the Fixed Penalty (accepting responsibility that an offence has taken place) which involves the assignment mark being cancelled to zero, with the assessment to be resubmitted at the next attempt number, and the module capped at the minimum pass mark.

Normally for a first offence, it is likely a student would be offered the Fixed Penalty (accepting responsibility that an offence has taken place) which involves the assignment mark being cancelled to zero, with the assessment to be resubmitted at the next attempt number, and the module capped at the minimum pass mark.

Normally for a first offence, it is likely a student would be offered the Fixed Penalty (accepting responsibility that an offence has taken place) which involves the assignment mark being cancelled to zero, with the assessment to be resubmitted at the next attempt number, and the module capped at the minimum pass mark.
Where a student is already out of attempts for an assessment, no further opportunity to resubmit is possible and the module will be failed.
A third offence (or a very serious earlier offence) may result in complete disqualification from the University.
A second offence may usually (but not always) attract a Second Level Fixed Penalty which involves cancelling of any previous marks and retaking the module, capped (with relevant fees).

definitions.quote: Academic Integrity, sometimes referred to as 'academic misconduct', is to do something which may result in an unpermitted academic advantage, either for yourself or for someone else.
Using another person's words or ideas without acknowledgement and submitting them for assessment as though it were your own work.
Work undertaken with others is submitted and passed off as solely the work of one person.
